title: US Debt Tops $40 Trillion: Even the Doves Are Turning Hawkish
dek: The 2010 paper claiming growth halves once debt exceeds 90% of GDP was used by politicians as a red line for over a decade; now even the dove economist who argued for bold spending calls herself a hawk, but no one can say where that line is.
why: Medium information density, but the second half's reversal of positions and the interest rate data are worth it. For understanding how the US debt debate evolved from 2010 to today, this episode is a clear recap.
who: Investors and founders watching macro, rates and Treasuries; anyone who wants to understand the origins of the "debt red line" debate and why even doves have changed their tune.
skip: The show intro at 0:00-1:00 and the NPR promo for other programs at 6:19-7:19 can be skipped.

points.h: The real fuse on the debt snowball is interest
points.body: The textbook worry isn't the debt itself, but that interest costs feed on themselves: pay more interest, the deficit grows; a bigger deficit pushes debt higher; next period's interest is even bigger, and so on compounding worse and worse. The other path is investors losing their appetite for Treasuries, forcing the government to keep raising rates to attract buyers, making the snowball roll faster. Neither of these feared outcomes happened after the financial crisis, and in hindsight the people who argued the government should spend more were on the right side of history — Karen Dynan even thinks it should have spent more and the recession could have been shorter.

points.h: The 90% line was read into the paper
points.body: The 2010 six-page paper by Reinhart and Rogoff, "Growth in a Time of Debt," studied decades of debt data from 20 advanced economies and concluded that when debt reaches 90% of GDP, growth is only half its normal level. But what the paper actually did was sort countries into four buckets — low, medium, high, and very high — with the very high bucket containing countries with debt far above 90%, and technically it said that this bucket, on average and over long periods, was associated with lower growth. Politicians and the media read it as a red line: "cross 90% and the economy crashes." The paper never said that.

points.h: An Excel error ignited the austerity fight
points.body: The debate the paper sparked raged in blogs and newspapers, with calls for austerity and belt-tightening on one side and warnings not to kill the recovery, not to stop spending now, on the other. Later, more debt-friendly economists published a piece pointing out a major error in the Excel spreadsheet Reinhart and Rogoff used, and the paper's final sentence said that since their findings were wrong, the austerity agendas in Europe and the US should be reassessed. Correcting the error weakened the claim everyone had seized on, but didn't overturn it — the updated paper still showed high debt generally associated with slower growth, just less steeply.

points.h: Low growth can also cause high debt
points.body: High debt being correlated with low growth doesn't mean high debt causes low growth. Andrea Presbitero points out the causality could run the other way: when the economy underperforms, policymakers want to stimulate it, which means public consumption and public investment, and one way to pay for that is borrowing — borrowing pushes debt up, so you see low growth and high debt in the data at the same time. He and his coauthors ultimately reached the same conclusion as most: based on empirical evidence, no definitive answer is possible, and causality may run both ways. Moreover, the debt threshold varies by country — it could be 90%, 45%, or 100% — and depends on who the creditors are, whether they're domestic or foreign investors, and whether the debt is short-term or long-term.

points.h: Rates at zero shelved the whole issue
points.body: What makes high debt destructive isn't the debt itself but the interest paid on it. After the financial crisis, global rates fell to near zero and stayed there for years, so many macroeconomists figured maybe there was no need to worry much about debt, and attention drifted away from the topic. Then the world changed twice: the pandemic and the spending that followed pushed debt even higher, and more importantly, rates rose again. Today the cost of holding a lot of debt for the US and other countries is much higher than five or six years ago, and the shelved question has become relevant again.

points.h: Rogoff says 91% and you're doomed is a misreading
points.body: Ken Rogoff is still annoyed by how the paper was interpreted. He says 90% was just their highest bucket, and they never said that at 91% you suddenly go to hell — that's like a 55 mph speed limit, you drive 56 and you'll crash the next minute. He thinks that interpretation was used and distorted polemically. But he also stresses that you can't therefore say there's no threshold and any level of debt is fine — that's crazy too. His basic intuition hasn't changed: constantly leveraging up is playing with fire, and the US trajectory needs adjusting, not just debt but also Social Security and Medicare.

points.h: The dove who argued for spending has flipped
points.body: Two years later, debt has grown by more than $4 trillion, the large tax cuts Congress passed in 2025 further reduced revenue, and interest alone costs over $1 trillion a year, a record. Karen Dynan, who thought spending was worth the risk back then, now says, "I'm a debt hawk now," because changes in financial markets, especially the interest rate on Treasury borrowing, make her think this is trickier than she thought two years ago. She describes it as walking on ice and comforting yourself that it hasn't cracked yet. Last week the 10-year Treasury rate hit its highest level since before the Great Recession, and the CBO projects debt will exceed 120% of GDP by 2036, higher than at any point in US history including World War II.

points.h: Rogoff puts the odds of a big problem above 50%
points.body: Rogoff thinks the biggest misconception is believing rates will stay low forever, and that if they're high for a while, it's just a nightmare that will pass. He says he thinks the probability of something very serious happening is greater than 50% — not the end of the world, a debt crisis isn't the end of the world, but something very significant will happen and we're not prepared. He also says we need to reflect on how wrong everyone was and for how long, because that belief hasn't disappeared — mainstream opinion leaders think basically the same now as they did then. As for the red line, neither economist can draw it, but both agree the solution is spending cuts, tax increases, or both, and that looks impossible to push through.

quotes.text: So the scary thing about high debt is that you can get a snowballing of debt because of interest costs. And when you're paying a lot of interest and then you're running a larger deficit because you're paying a lot of interest, that adds to the debt. And then you get to the next period and you have more debt. And then you have more interest. And so it just keeps compounding and getting worse and worse and worse.
It seems like we don't have a good way of knowing whether we're 5% away from the ice cracking or 50% away from the ice cracking.
The fact that Reinhardt and Rogoff's findings are wrong should therefore lead us to reassess the austerity agenda itself in both Europe and the United States.

But we didn't say that suddenly you go to the devil when you get to 91%. That's a little bit like saying if you're driving in a car in a 55-mile-an-hour speed limit and you go to 56, you're going to crash the next minute.
But I do want to qualify that a little bit by saying to say, therefore, there's no threshold. Therefore, any level of debt is fine. That's kind of nuts also.

I am a debt hawk now. Given how things have evolved, we have seen things happen in financial markets, particularly treasury borrowing rates, that have made me think this is a bigger challenge than I thought it was a couple years ago.

I do think that the odds that we have a very significant problem are bigger than 50-50. They're not the end of the world. And frankly, having a debt crisis is not the end of the world. But I think something very significant is going to happen and we're not ready for it.
